sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source represents the inner ridge of the inherited Umbria-Marche thrust system, possibly inverted and re-activated in the current extensional regime.
Following the 2016-17 central Italy seismic sequence, a growing amount of evidence suggests that the large-scale thrust systems, originated from the build-up of the Apennines during the Miocene, are currently experiencing kinematic inversion in the Quaternary extensional regime (Scognamiglio et al., 2018; Bonini et al., 2019; Buttinelli et al., 2021). The active role of the inherited thrust system in the current extensional regime has been also confirmed by analog model experiments (Del Ventisette et al., 2021).
This Source straddles the central part of the Umbria-Marche fold and thrust belt from NNW to SSE. During the Miocene this fault system controlled the onset of the anticlines along the inner ridge of the chain (among many others, Bally et al., 1986; Cello et al., 1997; Vai, 2001; Basili and Barba, 2007; Barchi et al., 1998) including, from north to south: the Montiego-Monte Nerone Anticline (Barchi et al., 1998; Mirabella et al., 2008; De Donatis et al., 2020), the Monte Catria anticline (Tavani et al., 2008), and the Monte Igno-Valnerina thrust system (Scisciani et al., 2014).
Historical and instrumental catalogues (ISIDe Working Group, 2007; Guidoboni et al., 2019; Rovida et al., 2021) show a very dense intermediate (4.5 < Mw < 5.0) to damaging seismicity within the region. Furthermore, this area of the Apennines has been the locus of numerous destructive earthquakes, including the 30 April 1279 (Mw 6.2) Appennino Umbro-Marchigiano, the 17 April and 22 September 1747 (Mw 6.1 and Mw 5.4, respectively) Appennino Umbro-Marchigiano, the 27 July 1751 (Mw 6.4) Appennino Umbro-Marchigiano, and the 3 June 1781 (Mw 6.5) Cagliese earthquakes.
